title: The Quiet Quitting Debate

words.def: To adjust or reset how much value or effort you assign to something.
words.ex: After the missed promotion, she recalibrated how much overtime she was willing to give.

words.def: A lack of interest, energy, or commitment.
words.ex: Falling survey scores were read as a sign of employee disengagement.

words.def: To formally arrange for a piece of work, such as research, to be carried out.
words.ex: The company commissioned a survey to understand why morale had dropped.

words.def: A correct or fair relationship in size, amount, or degree between things.
words.ex: His pay never rose in proportion to his growing workload.

idioms.def: To do more than what is expected or required.
idioms.ex: She used to go above and beyond, staying late almost every night.

idioms.def: To make a distinction between two things less clear.
idioms.ex: Remote work blurred the lines between office hours and personal time.

phrasalVerbs.def: to reset or adjust
phrasalVerbs.ex: Workers recalibrated their effort once overtime stopped paying off.

phrasalVerbs.def: to have its origin in
phrasalVerbs.ex: The trend traces back to years of unpaid overtime during burnout periods.

passage:
A few years ago, a simple phrase reshaped how people talked about work: "quiet quitting." Despite the name, it has nothing to do with actually resigning. It describes employees who stop going beyond their job description — no more unpaid overtime, no more answering emails at midnight, no more volunteering for extra projects. They still do their job well; they just stop doing more than that.

To some managers, this looked like a crisis of loyalty. Surveys were commissioned, op-eds were written, and consultants were hired to figure out why an entire generation seemed to have lost its "hustle." But a closer look suggests something less dramatic is going on. Many of the employees labelled quiet quitters say they are simply doing what their contract actually asks of them — nothing more, nothing less. What changed is not their effort, but their willingness to treat unpaid extra work as normal.

Part of this shift traces back to burnout. During periods of long hours and blurred boundaries between home and office, many workers found that going "above and beyond" rarely led to promotions or raises in proportion to the extra hours given. When the reward for over-delivering didn't match the cost, people quietly recalibrated. They didn't quit their jobs; they quit the unwritten expectation that a job should absorb their whole life.

Employers who have responded well to this shift have tended to do one of two things: either they have redesigned roles so that "extra" effort is actually rewarded through pay or promotion, or they have simply accepted that a fair day's work for a fair day's pay is a reasonable arrangement, not a symptom of disengagement. The employers who have responded worst are the ones who keep asking for more without changing what they offer in return, and then wonder why enthusiasm keeps declining.

questions.question: According to the passage, what does 'quiet quitting' actually describe?
options: A) Employees secretly planning to resign from their jobs.
B) Employees who do only what their job description requires, without extra unpaid effort.
C) Employees who perform poorly at their assigned tasks.
D) Employees who negotiate for higher pay before taking on new work.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The second paragraph says these employees are 'doing what their contract actually asks of them — nothing more, nothing less,' which matches option B exactly.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage explicitly says quiet quitting 'has nothing to do with actually resigning.'
• C: The passage says they 'still do their job well.'
• D: Negotiating pay before taking on work is not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

questions.question: The passage suggests that the main cause of quiet quitting is:
options: A) A general decline in the work ethic of younger employees.
B) A mismatch between the extra effort employees gave and the rewards they received for it.
C) Companies removing the option of working overtime.
D) Employees being unable to understand their job descriptions.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: Paragraph 3 states that when 'the reward for over-delivering didn't match the cost, people quietly recalibrated' — a direct statement of mismatch between effort and reward.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage never blames a decline in work ethic; in fact it argues the opposite explanation.
• C: Overtime is described as something employees stopped giving voluntarily, not something removed by companies.
• D: This is not mentioned or implied anywhere.

questions.question: What is the author's attitude toward employers who ask for more without changing what they offer?
options: A) Sympathetic, because rewarding extra effort is expensive.
B) Neutral, since the passage does not comment on employer behaviour.
C) Critical, suggesting they shouldn't be surprised that enthusiasm keeps falling.
D) Admiring, because they maintain high standards.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The final line says such employers 'wonder why enthusiasm keeps declining' in a clearly critical, slightly ironic tone — implying the answer should be obvious to them.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: There is no sympathy expressed for this group in the passage.
• B: The passage does comment directly and critically on this behaviour.
• D: Nothing in the tone suggests admiration; quite the opposite.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the overall structure of the passage?
options: A) It presents a phenomenon, offers a common explanation, then offers a more likely explanation and its consequences.
B) It lists several unrelated workplace trends in chronological order.
C) It argues that quiet quitting is a myth invented by the media.
D) It compares quiet quitting across different countries.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage introduces the term, mentions the panic/'crisis of loyalty' explanation, then offers the burnout-based explanation and discusses how employers have responded — matching option A's structure.

Why the others are wrong:
• B: The trends discussed are all connected to one central phenomenon, not a list of unrelated ones.
• C: The passage never claims quiet quitting is a myth; it treats it as a real, explainable shift.
• D: No international comparison appears in the passage.

questions.question: The tone of the passage can best be described as:
options: A) Alarmed and urgent.
B) Explanatory and mildly sympathetic to employees.
C) Purely statistical and detached.
D) Dismissive of employer concerns entirely.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage calmly explains the phenomenon and leans toward understanding the employee perspective (e.g., 'quietly recalibrated,' 'a fair day's work for a fair day's pay is a reasonable arrangement'), which is explanatory with mild sympathy.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: There is no urgency or alarm in the writing style.
• C: The passage uses reasoning and narrative, not statistics.
• D: Employer concerns are acknowledged, just found unconvincing when unaddressed — not dismissed outright.

title: Tearing Down the Highway

words.def: The state of being overcrowded or clogged, especially with traffic.
words.ex: Rush-hour congestion added forty minutes to her commute.

words.def: A change to the opposite direction, position, or decision.
words.ex: The city's decision to remove the highway was a striking reversal of earlier policy.

words.def: To spread something out differently across an area.
words.ex: Without the highway, traffic redistributed itself across several smaller streets.

words.def: To have the opposite effect to the one intended.
words.ex: Removing the road backfired in cities that offered no alternative transport.

idioms.def: To cut or force a path directly through something.
idioms.ex: The highway was carved through what had been a residential neighbourhood.

idioms.def: To create a dark or gloomy area, or figuratively, to have a negative effect on something.
idioms.ex: The elevated road cast a permanent shadow over the street below.

phrasalVerbs.def: to rely on something for support or a need
phrasalVerbs.ex: More residents came to depend on cars once the wider road was built.

phrasalVerbs.def: to omit or leave out a step
phrasalVerbs.ex: Cities that skipped the step of building alternatives saw the removal backfire.

passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the answer to traffic congestion seemed obvious: build a bigger road. Cities across the world carved elevated highways straight through their centres, often through the poorest neighbourhoods, on the promise that faster movement of cars would mean a faster, more modern city. Decades later, a growing number of those same cities are doing something that would once have seemed unthinkable — tearing the highways back down.

The reasoning behind this reversal rests on an idea traffic engineers call "induced demand." A wider road does not simply relieve existing congestion; it invites more cars onto it, because driving suddenly feels more convenient. Within a few years, the new lanes are just as congested as the old ones were, except now more people depend on cars to get around. Removing a highway, it turns out, can work in reverse: without the road, some trips simply stop happening, others shift to public transport, and traffic redistributes onto smaller streets without the predicted chaos.

There are other motivations too. Elevated highways cast neighbourhoods below into permanent shadow, cut communities off from their own waterfronts or parks, and depress property values along their length. When cities have removed them, replacing the space with parks, housing, or boulevards, the reclaimed land has often become some of the most desirable in the entire city — a reversal few residents living under the noise and exhaust of the old highway would have predicted.

None of this means removing a highway is simple. It requires investment in alternatives — buses, trains, safer cycling routes — so that the reduced road capacity doesn't just strand people who have no other way to get to work. Cities that have skipped this step have seen removal backfire. But where the alternatives exist, the pattern is strikingly consistent: less road, it turns out, is not always the same as less mobility.

questions.question: What does the term 'induced demand' refer to in the passage?
options: A) The tendency of drivers to demand better roads from local governments.
B) The idea that widening a road creates more traffic rather than relieving it.
C) A government policy requiring more highways to be built.
D) The economic demand for housing near highways.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage defines it directly: 'A wider road does not simply relieve existing congestion; it invites more cars onto it.'

Why the others are wrong:
• A: This is not what the term means in the passage; it's about traffic behaviour, not political demands.
• C: Induced demand is a traffic pattern, not a government policy.
• D: Housing demand is discussed separately later in the passage, not as part of this term.

questions.question: According to the passage, why can removing a highway sometimes reduce traffic problems rather than worsen them?
options: A) Because some trips stop happening altogether and others shift to public transport.
B) Because all drivers are legally required to use buses instead.
C) Because cars become more expensive to operate.
D) Because the removed land is immediately converted into new roads elsewhere.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: Paragraph 2 explains: 'some trips simply stop happening, others shift to public transport, and traffic redistributes onto smaller streets.'

Why the others are wrong:
• B: No legal requirement to use buses is mentioned.
• C: The cost of operating cars is never discussed in the passage.
• D: The reclaimed land is described as being used for parks or housing, not new roads.

questions.question: The passage mentions property values along former highways primarily to show that:
options: A) Highways are always good for the local economy.
B) Removing a highway can make the reclaimed area more desirable than it was before.
C) Property values are unrelated to transport infrastructure.
D) Cities should charge higher taxes near highways.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage says highways 'depress property values,' and after removal, the reclaimed land 'has often become some of the most desirable' — directly supporting option B.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage argues the opposite: highways depress property values.
• C: The whole point of this section is that they ARE related.
• D: Taxes are never mentioned in the passage.

questions.question: According to the last paragraph, what determines whether a highway removal succeeds or 'backfires'?
options: A) Whether the city also invests in alternatives like public transport and cycling routes.
B) Whether the highway was built before or after 1980.
C) The total length of the highway being removed.
D) Whether residents vote in favour of the removal.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage states that removal requires 'investment in alternatives... so that the reduced road capacity doesn't just strand people' and that skipping this step causes it to backfire.

Why the others are wrong:
• B: No date threshold is mentioned in the passage.
• C: Length of highway is never discussed as a factor.
• D: Voting is not mentioned as a factor in the passage.

questions.question: Which one of the following best captures the overall argument of the passage?
options: A) Highways should never be built in any city.
B) Removing a highway, when paired with transport alternatives, can reduce congestion and revive neighbourhoods, challenging the assumption that more roads mean more mobility.
C) Public transport is always cheaper to build than highways.
D) Cities that remove highways always see an immediate drop in traffic with no downsides.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: This captures both halves of the passage: the induced-demand argument for removal, and the caveat that alternatives are necessary — matching the passage's balanced conclusion.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage does not argue highways should never be built; it focuses on removal in specific cases.
• C: Relative construction costs are never compared in the passage.
• D: The passage explicitly notes removal can backfire without alternatives — so it is not free of downsides.

title: The Real Cost of a Free Return

words.def: To take on a cost without passing it to someone else or without visible effect.
words.ex: The company could no longer absorb the cost of unlimited free returns.

words.def: To accept a loss and stop trying to recover its value.
words.ex: It was cheaper to write off the item's cost than to process its return.

words.def: Not able to be seen, or in this context, hidden from obvious view.
words.ex: The true cost of free returns was invisible, hidden in slightly higher prices.

words.def: Giving a false or unclear impression.
words.ex: Calling the returns 'free' was somewhat misleading, since someone always paid for them.

idioms.def: Involving no danger of loss.
idioms.ex: Free returns were marketed as a risk-free way to shop online.

idioms.def: No longer appropriate for the current time of year; unable to be sold now.
idioms.ex: Returned winter coats sent back in spring are often out of season by the time they're processed.

phrasalVerbs.def: to return something to its source
phrasalVerbs.ex: Customers can send back items they don't want within thirty days.

phrasalVerbs.def: to include as part of a larger whole, often without drawing attention to it
phrasalVerbs.ex: The cost of returns was folded into slightly higher prices for everyone.

passage:
Free returns feel like one of the great conveniences of online shopping. Order three sizes, keep the one that fits, send the rest back at no charge — no risk, no cost. But the "free" in free returns has always been a little misleading. Someone pays for the shipping, the sorting, the repackaging, and often the disposal of items too damaged or out of season to resell. That someone is usually the retailer, and increasingly, the retailer has decided it can no longer absorb the cost quietly.

A returned item rarely goes straight back onto the shelf. It has to be inspected, cleaned, and repackaged, and each of these steps costs money and time. For low-priced items, the cost of processing a return can be higher than the item itself was worth, which is why a growing number of retailers now tell customers to simply keep unwanted items rather than send them back at all. It is often cheaper to write off the loss than to pay for the return journey.

What cannot be resold does not simply disappear. Investigations into returned goods have found that a significant share ends up in landfill, since sorting through every returned box for resale value takes more labour than most retailers are willing to fund. A shirt bought, tried on, and returned within a week may travel further in its short life than most people ever imagine.

In response, some retailers have begun charging small return fees, while others reward customers who buy carefully in the first place, such as by offering size-recommendation tools. The underlying message is the same: the true cost of a "risk-free" purchase was never actually zero. It was simply invisible, folded into slightly higher prices for everyone, until businesses decided it made more sense to make that cost visible instead.

questions.question: According to the passage, why is the word 'free' in 'free returns' considered misleading?
options: A) Because customers are secretly charged a hidden fee at checkout.
B) Because someone still pays for the shipping, processing, and disposal involved.
C) Because returns are no longer allowed at most stores.
D) Because only expensive items can be returned for free.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage says plainly that 'someone pays for the shipping, the sorting, the repackaging, and often the disposal' — the cost exists, it's just not charged directly to the customer.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: No hidden checkout fee is mentioned in the passage.
• C: The passage discusses returns changing, not disappearing.
• D: Price of the item is not presented as a condition for free returns.

questions.question: Why do some retailers now ask customers to keep unwanted items instead of returning them?
options: A) Because storage space in warehouses has run out.
B) Because processing a low-value return can cost more than the item itself is worth.
C) Because customers rarely want to return anything.
D) Because government regulations now require it.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage states this directly: 'the cost of processing a return can be higher than the item itself was worth,' making it cheaper to let the customer keep it.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: Warehouse space is not mentioned as an issue.
• C: The passage assumes returns are common, which is why the cost matters.
• D: No regulation is mentioned as a cause.

questions.question: What happens to many returned items that cannot be resold, according to the passage?
options: A) They are donated directly to charities.
B) They are sent back to the original manufacturer for a refund.
C) A significant share ends up in landfill.
D) They are relabelled and sold at full price.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage states plainly: 'a significant share ends up in landfill, since sorting through every returned box for resale value takes more labour than most retailers are willing to fund.'

Why the others are wrong:
• A: Donation is not mentioned in the passage.
• B: Returning to the manufacturer is not discussed.
• D: Reselling at full price contradicts the described process of items losing resale value.

questions.question: The overall tone of the passage toward the concept of 'free returns' is:
options: A) Outraged, condemning retailers for years of hidden costs.
B) Explanatory, revealing that a seemingly free convenience always carried a real, previously hidden cost.
C) Purely promotional, encouraging readers to shop online more.
D) Dismissive of any environmental concerns related to returns.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage calmly explains the mechanics behind 'free' returns without expressing outrage, while clearly stating the cost 'was never actually zero' — an explanatory tone revealing a hidden truth.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: There is no language of outrage or condemnation used.
• C: The passage is critical/analytical, not promotional of shopping.
• D: Environmental concerns (landfill) are directly discussed, not dismissed.

title: The Myth of Catching Up on Sleep

words.def: Easy to understand or seeming naturally obvious, without needing to think hard about it.
words.ex: The idea of repaying sleep debt on weekends feels intuitive, even if it isn't accurate.

words.def: The chemical processes in the body that convert food into energy.
words.ex: Chronic short sleep appears to disrupt metabolism in ways a single long sleep cannot fix.

words.def: The process of making something stronger or more solid, here referring to memory becoming stable in the brain.
words.ex: Sleep plays an important role in memory consolidation.

words.def: Raised to a higher level than normal.
words.ex: Markers of metabolic stress remained elevated even after a weekend of catch-up sleep.

idioms.def: To continue doing something difficult despite wanting to stop.
idioms.ex: She pushed through the week on very little sleep, planning to rest on the weekend.

idioms.def: To add more of something to bring it back to a fuller or desired level.
idioms.ex: He tried to top up his sleep with a long lie-in on Sunday.

phrasalVerbs.def: to sleep later than usual in the morning
phrasalVerbs.ex: Many people sleep in on weekends to make up for lost rest.

phrasalVerbs.def: to return to a previous state or habit
phrasalVerbs.ex: After the weekend, the body reverts to its early weekday alarm schedule.

passage:
Ask most people how they handle a short night of sleep, and the plan is usually the same: push through the week, then sleep in on Saturday. This idea of a "sleep debt" that can be repaid with a long weekend lie-in feels intuitive, almost like a bank account you can top up after overspending. Unfortunately, sleep researchers say the metaphor breaks down in an important way — sleep does not work quite like money.

Some of what sleep does for the brain and body can indeed be partly recovered with extra hours later. Reaction time and short-term alertness tend to improve after a long catch-up sleep, which is why an extra hour or two on the weekend does make people feel noticeably better. But other effects of chronic short sleep, particularly on metabolism, blood sugar regulation, and long-term memory consolidation, do not appear to reverse as neatly. Studies following people who slept five or six hours on weekdays and then slept in on weekends found that markers of metabolic stress remained elevated despite the "catch-up" sleep, as though the body had not fully forgiven the debt.

Part of the problem is that a single long sleep, however welcome, is not the same as several nights of consistently adequate rest. The body's internal clock also gets disrupted by the pattern itself: staying up late and sleeping in on weekends, then reverting to early alarms on Monday, produces a kind of mini jet lag that researchers sometimes call "social jet lag." That disruption carries its own costs, separate from the sleep debt it is meant to repay.

None of this means an extra hour of sleep on the weekend is pointless — tired brains will still take whatever rest is on offer, gladly. It simply means the healthiest solution to a persistent shortfall is not a single large repayment, but smaller, steadier deposits: consistent sleep across the whole week, rather than a large withdrawal followed by an attempted refund.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the main problem with the 'sleep debt' metaphor?
options: A) It suggests sleep can be fully repaid the same way money can, which does not match how the body actually recovers.
B) It implies that sleeping too much is dangerous.
C) It was invented by sleep researchers to sell sleep-tracking devices.
D) It applies only to people with medical sleep disorders.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage states the metaphor 'breaks down' because 'sleep does not work quite like money' — some effects recover, but others (metabolic, memory-related) do not, unlike a simple financial repayment.

Why the others are wrong:
• B: The passage never claims oversleeping is dangerous.
• C: No mention of sleep-tracking devices or commercial motives appears in the passage.
• D: The passage discusses this as a general pattern, not limited to people with sleep disorders.

questions.question: Which of the following effects of short sleep does the passage say does NOT fully recover with catch-up sleep?
options: A) Short-term alertness.
B) Reaction time.
C) Metabolic and blood sugar regulation.
D) Immediate feelings of tiredness.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage explicitly separates alertness and reaction time (which improve with catch-up sleep) from 'metabolism, blood sugar regulation, and long-term memory consolidation,' which 'do not appear to reverse as neatly.'

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage says alertness DOES improve with a catch-up sleep.
• B: Reaction time is listed among the things that do recover.
• D: General tiredness is not the specific effect being contrasted here.

questions.question: What is 'social jet lag' as described in the passage?
options: A) Jet lag experienced specifically while travelling for social events.
B) The disruption to the body's internal clock caused by sleeping late on weekends and waking early on weekdays.
C) A medical condition unrelated to sleep patterns.
D) The tiredness caused by socialising too much on weekends.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage defines it directly: the pattern of 'staying up late and sleeping in on weekends, then reverting to early alarms on Monday, produces a kind of mini jet lag that researchers sometimes call social jet lag.'

Why the others are wrong:
• A: It has nothing to do with travel; it's about weekday/weekend sleep timing.
• C: It is explicitly tied to sleep pattern disruption, not unrelated to sleep.
• D: It's about the schedule shift itself, not the act of socialising.

questions.question: What solution does the passage ultimately recommend for a persistent sleep shortfall?
options: A) Sleeping as much as possible every weekend to fully repay the debt.
B) Avoiding sleep entirely on weekdays to reset the body's clock.
C) Maintaining consistent, adequate sleep across the whole week rather than relying on one big weekend catch-up.
D) Relying on naps during the day instead of nighttime sleep.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The final paragraph states the healthiest solution is 'smaller, steadier deposits: consistent sleep across the whole week, rather than a large withdrawal followed by an attempted refund.'

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage argues this approach does not fully work, due to unresolved metabolic effects.
• B: This is not suggested anywhere and contradicts the passage's advice.
• D: Napping is not discussed as the recommended solution.

title: Four Days, Same Pay

words.def: Advocating or representing a fundamental or extreme change from what is usual or traditional.
words.ex: A four-day week without a pay cut once seemed like a radical proposal.

words.def: A person who argues in favour of something.
words.ex: Proponents of the shorter week point to steady productivity in the trials.

words.def: A person who tends to question or doubt claims that are generally accepted.
words.ex: Sceptics note that not every job can compress neatly into four days.

words.def: To press or squeeze something so that it takes up less space or time.
words.ex: The company tried to compress five days of work into four.

idioms.idiom: Close to a law of nature
idioms.def: Treated as an unquestionable, permanent fact, though not literally one.
idioms.ex: The five-day week was treated as close to a law of nature for decades.

idioms.idiom: Sound too convenient to be true
idioms.def: To seem suspiciously easy or beneficial, raising doubt about whether it's real.
idioms.ex: A shorter week with no pay cut sounds almost too convenient to be true.

phrasalVerbs.def: to remove or eliminate something
phrasalVerbs.ex: Compressing the week helps cut out low-value tasks that padded the day.

phrasalVerbs.def: to make something last longer than necessary
phrasalVerbs.ex: Some tasks were stretched out simply to fill the available working hours.

passage:
For over a century, the five-day working week has been treated as something close to a law of nature, even though it was itself once a radical proposal that factory owners resisted fiercely. In the past few years, a wave of companies across several countries has tried something that would have seemed equally radical: cutting the work week to four days, without cutting anyone's pay.

The results of the larger trials have been closely watched, partly because the idea sounds almost too convenient to be true. In several pilot programmes involving hundreds of companies, most participating businesses chose to continue with the shorter week once the trial period ended, citing steady or even improved output. Employees, unsurprisingly, reported lower stress and better sleep. What surprised some observers was that overall productivity, measured by output rather than hours logged, did not fall in most of these trials — and in a number of cases it rose.

The explanation offered by proponents is that a standard eight-hour day contains a great deal of low-value time: meetings that could have been an email, tasks stretched out to fill the available hours, and the general fatigue that builds up over a fifth consecutive day. Compress the working days and, the argument goes, people focus harder during the time they do have, cutting out the padding that a longer week quietly encourages.

Sceptics point out that not every job compresses this neatly. Roles that depend on continuous coverage, such as retail, healthcare, or manufacturing on fixed shifts, cannot simply eliminate a day of work without hiring more people to cover the gap, which raises costs in a way that office-based knowledge work does not face. For now, the four-day week remains most established among certain kinds of white-collar employers, with the harder test still ahead: whether the model can be adapted, rather than abandoned, for the jobs where a shift simply has to be staffed.

questions.question: According to the passage, what was surprising about the results of the four-day week trials?
options: A) Most companies immediately abandoned the trial after a few weeks.
B) Overall productivity did not fall, and in some cases rose, despite fewer working hours.
C) Employees reported more stress after switching to a shorter week.
D) Only a handful of companies agreed to participate.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage states plainly that 'overall productivity... did not fall in most of these trials — and in a number of cases it rose,' which is presented as the surprising finding.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage says most businesses chose to CONTINUE the shorter week, not abandon it.
• C: Employees reported LOWER stress, the opposite of this option.
• D: The passage mentions 'hundreds of companies' participating, not a small handful.

questions.question: What explanation do proponents give for why productivity can stay the same or improve with fewer working days?
options: A) Employees are paid less, so they work harder to compensate.
B) A standard work week contains low-value time that gets naturally cut when the week is compressed.
C) Companies hire more staff to cover the missing day.
D) Employees are legally required to complete the same output.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: Paragraph 3 explains that a standard day 'contains a great deal of low-value time,' and compressing the week forces people to 'focus harder... cutting out the padding.'

Why the others are wrong:
• A: Pay is explicitly NOT cut in these trials, as stated in the first paragraph.
• C: Hiring more staff is mentioned only as a challenge for shift-based jobs, not as the proponents' explanation.
• D: No legal requirement of this kind is mentioned.

questions.question: Why do sceptics doubt that the four-day week model can be applied everywhere?
options: A) Because employees generally dislike having an extra day off.
B) Because some jobs require continuous coverage and cannot simply lose a working day without extra hiring costs.
C) Because productivity data from the trials was never published.
D) Because the model has never been tested in any country.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage explains that roles needing 'continuous coverage, such as retail, healthcare, or manufacturing... cannot simply eliminate a day of work without hiring more people,' raising costs.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: There's no suggestion employees dislike time off — the opposite is implied.
• C: The passage describes detailed trial results, implying they were available/observed.
• D: The passage describes trials 'across several countries,' contradicting this option.

questions.question: The passage's overall stance on the four-day work week can best be described as:
options: A) Fully convinced it should replace the five-day week everywhere immediately.
B) Balanced — acknowledging its apparent success in some sectors while noting a real, unresolved challenge for others.
C) Entirely dismissive of the idea as unworkable.
D) Focused only on employee happiness, ignoring business outcomes.
questions.explanation:
Why this is correct: The passage presents encouraging trial results but ends by noting 'the harder test still ahead' for jobs requiring shift coverage — a balanced view rather than full endorsement or dismissal.

Why the others are wrong:
• A: The passage explicitly flags unresolved challenges, so it is not fully convinced of universal application.
• C: The passage reports largely positive results, so it is not dismissive.
• D: Business outcomes like productivity and cost are discussed extensively, not ignored.

title: Why We Tip

words.def: The freedom to decide something based on one's own judgement.
words.ex: The tip amount is left entirely to the diner's discretion.

words.def: To make an attitude or belief part of one's own way of thinking without conscious effort.
words.ex: Many diners have internalised tipping as a basic social obligation.

words.def: To formally put an end to a practice or institution.
words.ex: Some restaurants tried to abolish tipping altogether.

words.def: To bring something back after it had been removed.
words.ex: Several restaurants quietly reintroduced tipping after customer complaints.

idioms.def: To reduce or eliminate a difference between two amounts or states.
idioms.ex: Tips are expected to close the gap between the base wage and a livable income.

phrasalVerbs.def: to depend on or be based on something
phrasalVerbs.ex: The custom's survival rests on social pressure more than economic logic.

passage:
Tipping is one of the stranger customs in everyday economic life. In many countries, a diner pays not just for food but for an extra, unwritten amount decided entirely at their own discretion, based loosely on how good the service felt. Economists have long found this puzzling: if the amount is voluntary and paid after the service is already delivered, there is, in theory, nothing forcing anyone to pay it at all.

The custom's survival seems to rest less on economics than on social pressure. Diners tip partly because they expect to be judged if they don't, and partly because they've internalised tipping as simply what a decent person does. Servers, in turn, often depend on tips to make up a meaningful share of their income, particularly in countries where the base wage for tipped work is set lower than the standard minimum wage on the assumption that tips will close the gap.

This arrangement creates an odd dynamic: pay that should reward good service instead becomes an unpredictable, workplace-wide gamble affected by factors that have nothing to do with a server's skill — a slow kitchen, a large party's poor mood, or simply a quiet night with fewer generous tippers passing through. Some restaurants have experimented with abolishing tipping altogether, building a service charge into the menu price and paying staff a fixed, higher wage instead. Customer reaction to these experiments has been mixed: many diners say they prefer the fairness of a built-in charge, and yet several restaurants that removed tipping have quietly reintroduced it, reporting that guests missed the feeling of rewarding good service directly, however imperfect that reward system actually was.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do economists find tipping puzzling?
options: A) Because it is illegal in most countries.
B) Because it is a voluntary payment made after the service is already delivered, so nothing forces anyone to pay it.
C) Because restaurants make no profit from food sales.
D) Because servers do not want to receive tips.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains the puzzle directly: since the amount is 'voluntary and paid after the service is already delivered, there is, in theory, nothing forcing anyone to pay it at all.' None of the other options are mentioned in the passage.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest actually sustains the custom of tipping?
options: A) Government regulation requiring it.
B) Social pressure and an internalised sense of obligation, rather than economic logic.
C) The fact that food would otherwise be more expensive.
D) A universal law applied in every country.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states the custom's survival 'rests on... social pressure' and that diners have 'internalised tipping as simply what a decent person does' — this is the sustaining force described, not law or regulation.

questions.question: Why has customer reaction to restaurants abolishing tipping been described as 'mixed'?
options: A) Because prices increased dramatically at every restaurant that tried it.
B) Because some diners preferred the fairness of a built-in charge, while others missed directly rewarding good service.
C) Because most customers refused to eat at such restaurants.
D) Because servers protested against the change.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage gives both sides: 'many diners say they prefer the fairness of a built-in charge,' yet other restaurants reintroduced tipping because 'guests missed the feeling of rewarding good service directly' — exactly the mixed reaction in option B.

title: The Library That Refuses to Close

words.def: The state of no longer existing; a complete end.
words.ex: Twenty years ago, some predicted the extinction of public libraries.

words.def: To take on a function or responsibility, often gradually.
words.ex: Libraries absorbed the role of free public space as other options disappeared.

words.def: To try to do more than one is able to do successfully or is meant to do.
words.ex: Critics argue libraries have overreached by taking on social service functions.

words.def: To provide less money than is needed for something to function properly.
words.ex: Social services are often underfunded, leaving gaps that other institutions fill.

idioms.def: The first person or place someone turns to for help with something.
idioms.ex: The library has become a first point of contact for people seeking jobs.

phrasalVerbs.def: to protect an existing function against change or removal
phrasalVerbs.ex: Libraries adapted their services rather than simply defending old ones.

passage:
It would have been easy to predict, twenty years ago, that public libraries were heading for extinction. Every service a library offered seemed to have a faster digital replacement: search engines instead of reference desks, e-books instead of paperbacks, streaming instead of borrowed DVDs. And yet, in many cities, libraries have not only survived the digital age but expanded what they offer, often becoming busier than before.

Part of the explanation is that libraries were never really just about books. They were one of the few remaining public spaces where a person could spend hours without being expected to buy anything. As other free indoor spaces disappeared from city centres, libraries quietly absorbed that role, offering warmth, a chair, a bathroom, and a place to be during working hours, no purchase required.

Libraries have also adapted their services rather than simply defending old ones. Many now lend more than books: tools, musical instruments, and even seeds for a home garden. They host free classes on everything from coding to tax filing, and increasingly serve as a first point of contact for people looking for a job, filling out government forms, or simply needing internet access they cannot afford at home.

This expansion has not been free of controversy. Some argue that libraries have overreached, becoming a substitute for social services that governments underfund elsewhere, using library staff to do the work that specialised outreach services should be doing instead. Others counter that libraries are simply doing what they have always done: meeting whatever need for free, dignified public space actually exists in their community, whatever form that need happens to take in a given decade.

questions.question: According to the passage, why have libraries remained relevant despite digital alternatives to their traditional services?
options: A) Because e-books were banned in most countries.
B) Because they offer a free public space and have adapted their services to new community needs.
C) Because governments require citizens to visit libraries.
D) Because digital replacements turned out to be more expensive than books.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage highlights two things: libraries provide 'a place to be during working hours, no purchase required,' and they've expanded services like classes, tool-lending, and job-search help — matching option B. None of the other options appear in the passage.

questions.question: What is the main criticism of libraries mentioned in the final paragraph?
options: A) That they charge too much for membership.
B) That they have become too focused on lending books and ignore other needs.
C) That they are substituting for underfunded government social services.
D) That they no longer allow the public to enter for free.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states the criticism directly: libraries have 'become a substitute for social services that governments underfund elsewhere.' The other options are not supported by the passage.

questions.question: The overall tone of the passage toward the expansion of library services is:
options: A) Entirely critical, arguing libraries should return to lending only books.
B) Balanced, presenting both the value of the expansion and the controversy around it.
C) Purely celebratory, with no acknowledgment of any downside.
D) Indifferent, treating the topic as unimportant.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage describes the benefits of expansion in detail, then presents a genuine counter-argument ('has not been free of controversy') before offering a rebuttal — a balanced treatment rather than one-sided praise or criticism.

title: Why Flying Makes You Feel Strange

words.def: The internal, roughly 24-hour cycle that regulates sleep, alertness, and other bodily functions.
words.ex: Jet lag disrupts the body's natural circadian rhythm.

words.def: To cause things to happen or operate at the same time or rate.
words.ex: Under normal conditions, the body's systems stay synchronised with each other.

words.def: To adapt or adjust to fit new circumstances.
words.ex: The body accommodates a later bedtime more easily than an earlier one.

words.def: A situation in which two or more things do not correspond or fit together properly.
words.ex: Jet lag is caused by a mismatch between the internal clock and local time.

idioms.def: Deeply built into a system as a fundamental part of how it works.
idioms.ex: The circadian rhythm is wired into nearly every system in the body.

phrasalVerbs.def: to reach the same level or state as something else after lagging behind
phrasalVerbs.ex: Digestion can take over a week to catch up to the new time zone.

passage:
Jet lag has a reputation as a minor, almost comic inconvenience — a slightly groggy traveller struggling to stay awake at dinner or wide awake at 3 a.m. But the underlying cause is a genuinely significant mismatch between the body's internal clock and the world it suddenly finds itself in, and understanding why reveals something interesting about how deeply that clock is wired into nearly every system in the body.

Almost every cell in the human body runs on an approximate 24-hour cycle, known as the circadian rhythm, governed largely by a small cluster of neurons in the brain that respond primarily to light. This master clock tells the body when to release hormones that promote alertness, when to lower body temperature in preparation for sleep, and when to prepare the digestive system for a meal. Under normal conditions, all of these systems stay neatly synchronised with each other and with the outside world.

Long-haul flight breaks that synchronisation abruptly. The light cues at the destination say it is morning; the internal clock, still running on the old time zone, insists it is the middle of the night. Different bodily systems also resynchronise at different speeds — sleep-related hormones often adjust within a few days, while digestion and body temperature can take over a week to fully catch up. This is why travellers can feel approximately fine but still find their appetite oddly timed or their energy dipping unpredictably, well after the obvious sleepiness has faded.

Interestingly, the direction of travel matters. Most people find it easier to adjust after flying westward, since this simply requires staying up later, something the body's natural rhythm accommodates fairly easily. Flying eastward requires forcing sleep earlier than the body wants, working against the clock rather than gently extending it — which is part of why an eastbound flight home so often feels harder than the outbound trip did.

questions.question: According to the passage, what actually causes the symptoms of jet lag?
options: A) A shortage of oxygen during long flights.
B) A mismatch between the body's internal 24-hour clock and the light and time cues at the new destination.
C) Dehydration caused by cabin air.
D) The stress of travelling through airports.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage attributes jet lag directly to the internal clock being out of sync with 'the world it suddenly finds itself in' — described in detail as a mismatch between light cues and the internal clock. The other listed causes are never mentioned.

questions.question: Why might a traveller feel 'approximately fine' but still notice unusual appetite or energy dips well after arrival?
options: A) Because different bodily systems (like digestion) resynchronise at different speeds than others (like sleep hormones).
B) Because airline food schedules are deliberately irregular.
C) Because the traveller has developed a permanent illness.
D) Because caffeine consumption increases during travel.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains that 'sleep-related hormones often adjust within a few days, while digestion and body temperature can take over a week' — different systems catching up at different rates explains the lingering odd symptoms.

questions.question: According to the passage, why is eastward travel generally harder to adjust to than westward travel?
options: A) Eastward flights are always longer in distance.
B) Eastward travel requires forcing sleep earlier than the body naturally wants, while westward travel simply requires staying up later.
C) Airlines provide worse service on eastbound routes.
D) Eastward travel crosses more time zones on average.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states westward travel 'simply requires staying up later, something the body's natural rhythm accommodates fairly easily,' while eastward travel means 'forcing sleep earlier than the body wants' — a harder adjustment.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the main idea of the passage?
options: A) Jet lag is a purely psychological phenomenon with no physical basis.
B) Jet lag reflects a real disruption to the body's internal 24-hour clock, with different systems recovering at different speeds depending on direction of travel.
C) Long-haul flights should be avoided entirely due to health risks.
D) All bodily systems resynchronise instantly upon arrival at a new destination.
questions.explanation: Explanation: This captures the passage's central explanation: the circadian mismatch, the staggered recovery of different systems, and the westward/eastward asymmetry. The other options either contradict the passage or overstate its claims.

title: The Loud Room Problem

words.def: The action of working with someone to produce or create something.
words.ex: Open-plan offices were meant to increase collaboration between colleagues.

words.def: To withdraw or move back, here in a figurative sense of pulling away socially.
words.ex: Employees often retreat into headphones rather than engage in noisy open offices.

words.def: The state of keeping careful watch or attention, often due to alertness to a possible threat.
words.ex: Constant visibility in an open office can trigger a low-grade sense of vigilance.

words.def: The outward appearance or impression of something, often not entirely genuine or complete.
words.ex: Employees used headphones to preserve some semblance of privacy.

idioms.def: Presented or marketed as something, often implying the reality may differ.
idioms.ex: Open-plan offices were sold as a way to increase collaboration.

phrasalVerbs.def: to remove or demolish, literally or figuratively
phrasalVerbs.ex: The design knocked down physical walls to encourage interaction.

passage:
Open-plan offices were sold, over two decades ago, as a way to boost collaboration by knocking down the walls between colleagues. The pitch was simple: remove barriers, and ideas will flow more freely between desks. What has actually followed, according to a large body of workplace research, is a somewhat different story — one where quieter, more focused employees have often paid the highest price for a design built around a louder ideal of teamwork.

Studies tracking real offices before and after a switch to open-plan layouts have found that face-to-face interaction, the very thing the design was meant to increase, often falls rather than rises. Faced with constant visibility and noise, many employees respond not by talking more, but by retreating further: putting on headphones, avoiding eye contact, and communicating over email or chat even with someone sitting a few metres away, simply to preserve some semblance of privacy and focus.

Introverted employees, and anyone doing work that requires sustained concentration, tend to report the sharpest drop in satisfaction. Being constantly visible and audible to colleagues activates a kind of low-grade vigilance that is mentally tiring over a full working day, even when nothing overtly stressful is happening. Extroverted employees, by contrast, often report the open layout more positively, since ambient activity and easy conversation suit their preferred way of working.

Some companies have responded by building a mix of spaces rather than committing to one layout for everyone: open areas for genuine collaborative work, alongside quiet rooms or phone booths for focused, individual tasks. The lesson many workplace designers now draw is less about which layout is objectively best, and more about the mistake of assuming one office design could ever suit every kind of worker equally well.

questions.question: According to the passage, what was the original justification for open-plan offices?
options: A) To reduce office rent costs.
B) To increase collaboration by removing physical barriers between employees.
C) To make offices quieter for concentration.
D) To reduce the number of employees needed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states the pitch directly: 'remove barriers, and ideas will flow more freely between desks' — the stated goal was increased collaboration, not cost, quiet, or staffing.

questions.question: What surprising outcome does the passage report regarding face-to-face interaction in open offices?
options: A) It increased dramatically, exceeding expectations.
B) It often fell, as employees retreated into headphones and digital communication instead.
C) It remained exactly the same as before the redesign.
D) It only changed for employees working night shifts.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states plainly that 'face-to-face interaction... often falls rather than rises,' with employees using 'headphones' and 'email or chat' instead — directly matching option B.

questions.question: Why do introverted employees report the sharpest drop in satisfaction in open offices, according to the passage?
options: A) They dislike using computers.
B) Constant visibility and noise create a mentally tiring, low-grade vigilance.
C) They are given less desk space than extroverted colleagues.
D) They are required to work longer hours.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains that being 'constantly visible and audible... activates a kind of low-grade vigilance that is mentally tiring,' particularly for those needing sustained concentration.

title: The Hidden Mathematics of Waiting in Line

words.def: The feeling of annoyance, especially something persistent.
words.ex: Waiting in line causes a mild but persistent irritation for most people.

words.def: Filled with activity, in this context referring to time spent doing something rather than nothing.
words.ex: Occupied time in a queue feels shorter than unoccupied, idle waiting.

words.def: Larger or more extreme than is reasonable or justified given the actual cause.
words.ex: The frustration from a slower line is often out of proportion to the actual time lost.

words.def: Extremely harsh, difficult, or unpleasant to endure.
words.ex: Uncertainty about wait times can be the most punishing factor of all.

idioms.def: Not matching the actual size or seriousness of something; excessive.
idioms.ex: Her anger was out of proportion to the small delay she experienced.

phrasalVerbs.def: to direct a path so that it passes by a particular place
phrasalVerbs.ex: Amusement parks route queues past entertaining scenery to make waits feel shorter.

passage:
Few experiences unite people across cultures as reliably as the mild irritation of standing in a queue. What is less obvious is how much careful thought goes into designing the lines themselves, and how the same waiting time can feel dramatically different depending on decisions most customers never notice they're reacting to.

One well-documented finding is that occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time. A queue that winds past shop windows, or a bank that provides a screen with light entertainment, will be rated as faster by customers than an identical wait spent staring at a blank wall, even when the clock says otherwise. This is why airports place duty-free shops along the route to boarding gates, and why some amusement parks route queues past deliberately entertaining scenery rather than the shortest possible path.

Fairness matters just as much as speed. A single winding line that feeds multiple service counters, the system now common in banks and airport check-ins, is usually rated as fairer and less stressful than several separate lines, even when the average waiting time is mathematically identical. The reason is straightforward: in separate lines, a customer can watch another line move faster than their own, and that visible unfairness creates frustration out of proportion to the actual time lost.

Uncertainty is perhaps the most punishing factor of all. Studies consistently find that a wait with a known, displayed estimated time feels shorter and less stressful than a wait of the same length with no information at all, even when the estimate turns out to be slightly wrong. This is why so many modern systems, from ride-hailing apps to hospital waiting rooms, now display a countdown, even an imperfect one — not because it changes how long anyone actually waits, but because it changes how that same wait is experienced.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do airports place duty-free shops along the route to boarding gates?
options: A) To increase security checks along the way.
B) Because occupied time, such as browsing shops, feels shorter than unoccupied waiting time.
C) Because airports are legally required to include shops near gates.
D) To reduce the total distance travellers must walk.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains that 'occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time,' and directly cites duty-free shop placement as an application of this finding.

questions.question: Why is a single winding line feeding multiple counters generally rated as fairer than several separate lines?
options: A) It is always mathematically faster than separate lines.
B) It prevents customers from seeing another line move faster than their own, removing a source of visible unfairness.
C) It requires fewer staff to manage.
D) It is used only in airports, not in banks.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states the reason clearly: 'in separate lines, a customer can watch another line move faster than their own, and that visible unfairness creates frustration' — a single line removes this comparison. Speed is described as mathematically identical, not faster, ruling out option A.

questions.question: What is the main effect of displaying an estimated wait time, according to the passage?
options: A) It always makes the actual wait time shorter.
B) It makes the wait feel shorter and less stressful, even if the estimate is slightly wrong.
C) It has no measurable effect on how people experience waiting.
D) It is only effective in hospital waiting rooms.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states plainly that a wait with a displayed estimate 'feels shorter and less stressful... even when the estimate turns out to be slightly wrong' — it changes perception of the wait, not its actual length.

title: How a Rumour Becomes a Legend

words.def: The ability of something to last a long time without significant change.
words.ex: The durability of urban legends has less to do with truth than with story structure.

words.def: To regard something as being caused by or belonging to a particular source.
words.ex: The rumour was attributed to a friend of a friend, making it hard to verify.

words.def: Prepared in advance to react to something in a particular way.
words.ex: Listeners were already primed to worry about contamination before hearing the story.

words.def: A humorous or malicious deception, often widely believed.
words.ex: Modern viral hoaxes spread in a pattern similar to older urban legends.

idioms.def: An unnamed, unverifiable source used to lend credibility to a rumour.
idioms.ex: The story was always said to have happened to a friend of a friend.

phrasalVerbs.def: to make use of an existing feeling or resource
phrasalVerbs.ex: The legend tapped into an existing fear of contamination.

passage:
Long before social media existed, stories about alligators in the sewers, poisoned trick-or-treat candy, and stolen kidneys in hotel bathtubs spread across entire countries with remarkable speed and consistency, despite having no credible source and, in most cases, no basis in fact whatsoever. Folklorists who study these urban legends have found that their durability has less to do with truth than with a specific, repeatable structure that makes them easy to retell.

The most persistent legends tend to share a few features. They are almost always attributed to a friend of a friend rather than a named, checkable source, which makes them impossible to verify while still feeling personally credible. They also tap into an existing, often unspoken anxiety — about strangers, hidden contamination, or lost control over one's own body — meaning the story confirms something the listener was already primed to worry about, rather than introducing an entirely new fear.

Retelling also changes the story in a predictable direction. Details that make the story more dramatic, more specific, or more emotionally satisfying tend to survive each retelling, while dull or inconvenient details are quietly dropped. A vague, unremarkable warning gradually sharpens into a specific, vivid scene over dozens of retellings, in much the same way a photocopy loses detail with each successive copy, except that here the change runs in the opposite direction: toward increasing narrative clarity rather than decay.

Modern misinformation research has found that today's viral hoaxes on social media follow nearly the same underlying pattern, just at far greater speed. The technology has changed enormously; the psychological ingredients that make a false story spread — an unverifiable source, a pre-existing fear, and a satisfying narrative shape — appear to have changed hardly at all.

questions.question: According to the passage, why is attributing a story to a 'friend of a friend' effective for spreading it?
options: A) It makes the story legally binding.
B) It makes the story impossible to verify while still feeling personally credible.
C) It guarantees the story is completely true.
D) It requires the listener to contact the original source.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains this directly: the vague attribution 'makes it impossible to verify while still feeling personally credible' — that combination is what makes it effective, not truth or legal standing.

questions.question: What happens to the details of an urban legend as it gets retold many times, according to the passage?
options: A) The story becomes shorter and vaguer with each retelling.
B) Dramatic and emotionally satisfying details tend to survive, while dull details are dropped.
C) The story is retold in exactly the same words every time.
D) Retelling has no effect on which details remain.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states that 'details that make the story more dramatic, more specific, or more emotionally satisfying tend to survive each retelling, while dull or inconvenient details are quietly dropped.'

questions.question: The comparison to a photocopy in the third paragraph is used to illustrate that:
options: A) Urban legends lose detail and clarity with each retelling, just like a photocopy.
B) Urban legends become sharper and more vivid with each retelling, unlike a photocopy which loses detail.
C) Urban legends are printed and distributed like photocopies.
D) Photocopiers were originally invented to spread rumours.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explicitly contrasts the two: it says the change 'runs in the opposite direction' to a photocopy — legends sharpen 'toward increasing narrative clarity' with retelling, while a photocopy loses detail.

questions.question: According to the passage, what do modern viral hoaxes have in common with older urban legends?
options: A) Both rely on an unverifiable source, a pre-existing fear, and a satisfying narrative shape.
B) Both are spread exclusively through printed newspapers.
C) Both are proven to be completely true in most cases.
D) Both take decades to spread across a country.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The final paragraph states the shared 'psychological ingredients... an unverifiable source, a pre-existing fear, and a satisfying narrative shape — appear to have changed hardly at all,' only the speed of spread has changed.

title: The Mall Is Not Quite Dead

words.def: Large and empty, like a cave, often used to describe a big, echoing space.
words.ex: The cavernous mall corridors felt eerily quiet with so many stores closed.

words.def: A quick, simplified way of referring to a more complex idea.
words.ex: The struggling mall became shorthand for the decline of retail in general.

words.def: Able to be exchanged or substituted for one another without difference.
words.ex: Generic clothing items are largely interchangeable between different retailers.

words.def: To perform or progress in a particular way.
words.ex: Malls focused on entertainment have fared far better than purely retail ones.

idioms.def: To maintain one's position despite pressure or difficulty.
idioms.ex: Experience-focused malls have held their ground against online competition.

phrasalVerbs.def: to try to win or succeed based on a specific factor
phrasalVerbs.ex: Malls stopped competing on convenience and started competing on experience.

passage:
For years, the American shopping mall has served as a shorthand for retail decline: cavernous buildings, empty storefronts, fountains no longer running, all attributed to the unstoppable rise of online shopping. The story is not entirely wrong, but it is considerably less complete than the popular version suggests, and the full picture reveals more about what a mall was actually for than the "online shopping killed it" headline ever captures.

Online shopping certainly hurt malls that relied on generic mid-range clothing retailers, the kind of store easily replaced by a website with a bigger selection and free delivery. But malls that positioned themselves differently, either as luxury shopping destinations or as full-day entertainment venues with cinemas, restaurants, arcades, and gyms, have generally fared far better. The common thread among the survivors is that they stopped competing with the internet on convenience, something a mall was never going to win, and started competing on experience, something a website still struggles to replicate.

This shift reflects something economists call the "experience economy": as more goods become interchangeable and available instantly online, people increasingly pay for the parts of a purchase, or a day out, that cannot simply be shipped to their door. A meal with friends, a film on a large screen, or the simple pleasure of browsing without intent are difficult to compress into a delivery box, which is precisely why malls built around those experiences have held their ground while malls built purely around shopping have not.

The mall, in other words, is not disappearing so much as being sorted — into those that adapted to sell something the internet cannot, and those that continued selling only what the internet always could, and always would, do better.

questions.question: According to the passage, which kind of mall was hurt most by online shopping?
options: A) Malls built around luxury shopping and entertainment.
B) Malls relying on generic mid-range clothing retailers easily replaced by websites.
C) Malls located in small towns only.
D) Malls that closed before the internet existed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states plainly that online shopping 'hurt malls that relied on generic mid-range clothing retailers, the kind of store easily replaced by a website.' Luxury and entertainment-focused malls are described as faring better, the opposite of option A.

questions.question: What does the passage mean by malls competing 'on experience' rather than 'on convenience'?
options: A) Malls now offer faster home delivery than websites.
B) Malls offer things like meals, films, and browsing that cannot easily be replicated by online shopping.
C) Malls have reduced their prices below online retailers.
D) Malls now operate exclusively online.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage lists these exact examples — 'a meal with friends, a film on a large screen, or the simple pleasure of browsing' — as things 'difficult to compress into a delivery box,' i.e., the experiential offering online shopping can't match.

questions.question: What is the main point the passage makes about the future of malls?
options: A) All malls will inevitably close within the next decade.
B) Malls are being sorted into those that adapted to offer something the internet cannot, and those that did not.
C) Online shopping has had no real effect on malls at all.
D) Only malls in major cities will survive.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The final line states directly: the mall 'is not disappearing so much as being sorted — into those that adapted... and those that continued selling only what the internet always could... do better.'

title: The Price of 'Free' Apps

words.def: To combine many separate items of data into a single collection or total.
words.ex: Individual searches are aggregated into a detailed profile of user behaviour.

words.def: To support financially, often making something cheaper or free for the end user.
words.ex: Advertising revenue subsidises many free apps and services.

words.def: Giving the impression that something harmful or evil is happening.
words.ex: The data-collection arrangement is not automatically sinister on its own.

words.def: The act of making new or secret information known.
words.ex: Regulators have focused on improving the clarity of data disclosure.

idioms.def: The means or system by which something is transmitted or provided.
idioms.ex: The app functions as a delivery mechanism for user data, not just a service.

phrasalVerbs.def: to relocate a hidden expense to a less visible place
phrasalVerbs.ex: The cost of a free app is simply moved somewhere less visible than a price tag.

passage:
Very few things in a functioning economy are actually free, and the mobile apps millions of people download without paying a cent are no exception. The absence of a price tag does not mean the absence of a cost; it usually means the cost has simply been moved somewhere less visible, and paid in a currency other than money.

The most common arrangement is straightforward, even if it is rarely stated plainly: the app is free to download because the user's attention, and often their personal data, is the actual product being sold, typically to advertisers. Every minute spent scrolling, every location logged, and every search performed can be aggregated, packaged, and sold on to businesses trying to predict and influence what that user might buy next. The app itself is essentially the delivery mechanism for that data, not the end product it appears to be.

This arrangement is not automatically sinister — plenty of genuinely useful free services exist precisely because advertising revenue subsidises them, letting people access maps, communication tools, and information they otherwise could not afford. The concern raised by researchers and regulators is less about the existence of this trade and more about how clearly, or unclearly, it is disclosed. Long, dense privacy policies that almost no one reads in full technically inform users of what is collected, while functionally ensuring that very few of them actually understand it.

Some jurisdictions have begun requiring clearer, shorter disclosures and giving users more direct control over what is collected. Whether this closes the gap between technical consent and genuine understanding remains an open question, but it reflects a growing recognition that "free" was always doing a great deal of quiet work to describe an arrangement in which money was never really the point.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the 'actual product' being sold in many free apps?
options: A) The app's source code, sold to competing developers.
B) The user's attention and personal data, typically sold to advertisers.
C) Physical goods advertised within the app.
D) Government contracts related to app development.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states this directly: 'the user's attention, and often their personal data, is the actual product being sold, typically to advertisers.' The other options are not mentioned.

questions.question: What concern do researchers and regulators raise about this data arrangement, according to the passage?
options: A) That collecting any data at all should be made completely illegal.
B) That the arrangement is inherently sinister and should be banned outright.
C) That the disclosure of this trade, through long privacy policies, technically informs users without them genuinely understanding it.
D) That free apps should be required to charge a fee instead.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states the concern is 'less about the existence of this trade and more about how clearly, or unclearly, it is disclosed,' noting privacy policies 'technically inform users... while functionally ensuring that very few of them actually understand it.'

questions.question: The passage's overall stance on free apps funded by advertising is best described as:
options: A) Entirely condemning, arguing all such apps should be banned.
B) Nuanced — acknowledging real benefits while raising a specific concern about disclosure and understanding.
C) Fully approving, with no concerns raised at all.
D) Focused only on the technical workings of mobile advertising.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explicitly states the arrangement 'is not automatically sinister' and lists genuine benefits, while still raising a clear, specific concern about disclosure — a nuanced, balanced stance rather than outright condemnation or approval.

title: Confident, and Confidently Wrong

words.def: An exaggerated sense of one's own importance or ability.
words.ex: The pattern is more dangerous than obvious arrogance because it looks like real competence.

words.def: To judge something to be smaller, less important, or less capable than it actually is.
words.ex: Experts often underestimate how much they know relative to others.

words.def: A lack of equality or balance between two things.
words.ex: This asymmetry between confidence and competence has real workplace consequences.

words.def: Not deserved or justified by effort or ability.
words.ex: The unskilled person's confidence is unearned by their actual understanding.

idioms.def: Hidden complexity not immediately visible or obvious.
idioms.ex: Experts understand how much complexity lies beneath any seemingly simple question.

phrasalVerbs.def: to judge or assess one's own ability or performance
phrasalVerbs.ex: Unskilled individuals tend to rate their own ability more generously than experts do.

passage:
There is a particular kind of confidence that should worry us more than obvious arrogance, precisely because it is so easy to mistake for competence. Psychologists have long documented a pattern in which people with the least skill or knowledge in a given area tend to rate their own ability the most generously, while genuine experts, more aware of the field's complexity, often underestimate how much they actually know relative to others.

The explanation is not that unskilled people are simply arrogant by nature. Rather, the same lack of skill that produces poor performance also removes the very tool needed to recognise poor performance: judgement. Correctly assessing how good an answer is requires much of the same knowledge needed to produce a good answer in the first place. A person who cannot yet distinguish a strong argument from a weak one has no reliable internal signal telling them that their own argument might be weak, so they proceed with a confidence unearned by their actual grasp of the subject.

Experts, meanwhile, face an almost opposite problem. Having spent years discovering how much complexity exists beneath any seemingly simple question, they tend to assume that other people find the same subtleties equally obvious, and so they often undervalue their own relative expertise compared to peers who seem just as confident, even when that confidence is built on far shallower foundations.

This asymmetry has practical consequences beyond mildly awkward dinner-table debates. In workplaces, the loudest, most confident voice in a meeting is not reliably the most informed one, and organisations that promote based on displayed confidence rather than demonstrated competence risk consistently rewarding exactly the wrong signal. The uncomfortable lesson is that confidence, on its own, tells you almost nothing about whether the confident person is actually right.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do unskilled people tend to overrate their own ability?
options: A) Because they are naturally more arrogant than skilled people.
B) Because the same lack of skill that causes poor performance also removes the ability to judge that performance accurately.
C) Because they receive more praise from others than skilled people do.
D) Because they have never attempted the task before.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage rejects the arrogance explanation directly ('The explanation is not that unskilled people are simply arrogant') and instead explains that 'the same lack of skill... also removes the very tool needed to recognise poor performance: judgement.'

questions.question: Why do experts, according to the passage, sometimes underestimate their own relative expertise?
options: A) Because they lack confidence in general, in every area of life.
B) Because they assume others find the same subtleties in a subject equally obvious.
C) Because they have less knowledge than they think.
D) Because they are punished for expressing confidence at work.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains that experts 'tend to assume that other people find the same subtleties equally obvious,' leading them to undervalue their own expertise relative to more confident but less knowledgeable peers.

questions.question: What practical risk does the passage identify in workplaces regarding this pattern?
options: A) That workplaces might promote people based on displayed confidence rather than actual competence.
B) That confident employees are always the most competent.
C) That quiet employees are never given opportunities to speak.
D) That workplaces eliminate meetings entirely to avoid this problem.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage states plainly: 'organisations that promote based on displayed confidence rather than demonstrated competence risk consistently rewarding exactly the wrong signal.'

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: A) Confidence and competence are always closely aligned in most people.
B) A lack of skill can prevent a person from recognising their own lack of skill, making confidence an unreliable signal of actual ability.
