C) Experts are always more confident than beginners in any field.
D) Arrogance is the root cause of most workplace failures.
questions.explanation: Explanation: This captures the passage's core claim, stated in its final line: 'confidence, on its own, tells you almost nothing about whether the confident person is actually right.' The other options either contradict the passage or oversimplify its argument.

title: Too Many Good Options

words.def: Relating to mental processes such as thinking, understanding, and reasoning.
words.ex: Comparing many options requires real cognitive effort.

words.def: To gradually wear away or diminish something over time.
words.ex: Lingering doubt about rejected options can erode confidence in a decision already made.

words.def: Carefully selected and organised, often to improve quality or ease of use.
words.ex: A curated menu with fewer options often leads to higher satisfaction.

words.def: To keep something going or maintain it over time.
words.ex: Comparing dozens of options became too exhausting to sustain.

idioms.def: To resort to something as a default when other options seem too difficult.
idioms.ex: Overwhelmed customers often fall back on a default option rather than compare everything.

phrasalVerbs.def: to be greater or more significant than something else
phrasalVerbs.ex: Past a certain point, the cost of extra choice outweighs its benefit.

passage:
It seems obvious that having more choices should make people happier: more flavours, more career paths, more possible routes to take. Yet a substantial body of research in behavioural psychology suggests that beyond a certain point, additional choice does not make decisions easier or more satisfying — it makes them harder, slower, and often less satisfying once made.

The mechanism behind this has become known as the paradox of choice. Comparing many similar options requires real cognitive effort, and as the number of alternatives grows, so does the mental cost of evaluating them properly. Faced with an overwhelming menu, many people either delay the decision altogether or fall back on a default option, not because it is genuinely the best fit, but because continuing to compare alternatives has simply become too exhausting to sustain.

Even after a decision is made, more options tend to lower satisfaction with the choice actually taken. With only two or three alternatives, a person who commits to one can be reasonably confident it was a good pick. With thirty alternatives, it becomes far more likely that at least one of the rejected options would have been slightly better in some way, and that lingering possibility quietly erodes confidence in the choice that was made, even when the chosen option is perfectly satisfactory on its own terms.

This research has practical implications well beyond grocery aisles. Retirement fund providers who offer fewer, carefully curated investment options often see higher enrolment than those offering dozens of near-identical funds. Restaurants with shorter, more curated menus frequently report higher customer satisfaction than those offering pages of options. The lesson is not that choice itself is bad, but that past a certain point, the value of an additional option is outweighed by the mental cost of considering it.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is the 'paradox of choice'?
options: A) The idea that people always prefer having fewer options than more.
B) The finding that beyond a certain point, more choices make decisions harder and less satisfying rather than easier.
C) The observation that people never make decisions when given any choice at all.
D) A mathematical rule about how many options a menu should contain.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage defines it directly: 'beyond a certain point, additional choice does not make decisions easier or more satisfying — it makes them harder, slower, and often less satisfying.'

questions.question: Why does having thirty alternatives tend to lower satisfaction compared to having two or three, according to the passage?
options: A) Because larger menus are always more expensive.
B) Because it becomes more likely that a rejected option was slightly better, which erodes confidence in the choice made.
C) Because people are physically unable to read that many options.
D) Because retailers deliberately make larger menus confusing.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage explains: with more alternatives, 'it becomes far more likely that at least one of the rejected options would have been slightly better in some way, and that lingering possibility quietly erodes confidence.'

questions.question: What practical lesson does the passage draw from research on retirement funds and restaurant menus?
options: A) Businesses should always offer as many options as possible.
B) Past a certain point, the value of an additional option is outweighed by the mental cost of considering it.
C) Retirement funds and restaurants should never offer any choice to customers.
D) Curated menus are only effective in the restaurant industry.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The final line states this directly: 'the value of an additional option is outweighed by the mental cost of considering it' — illustrated by both the retirement fund and restaurant menu examples.
